title: The Pull and the Cuts: One Receptor, One Message

scenes.visual: Title card over the carried two-cell world already gently breathing: cross-section of a sending cell above (warm amber membrane) and a receiving cell below (cool teal membrane), with a deep indigo nucleus at the bottom. High-contrast title: 'The Pull and the Cuts: One Receptor, One Message'. Ambient shimmer along both membranes.

scenes.tts: Without Notch, a fly embryo builds too much nervous system and too little skin. How does one cell tell a touching neighbour, not you? Its signal never leaves the sending cell.
scenes.caption: Without Notch, a fly embryo builds too much nervous system and too little skin. How does one cell tell a touching neighbour, “not you”? Its signal never leaves the sending cell.
scenes.visual: The title fades; the two touching cells expand to fill 70% of the frame height. Above, a warm amber sending cell; below, a cool teal receiving cell with its deep indigo nucleus visible at the base. A small schematic callout on the left briefly contrasts balanced nerve-and-skin dots versus an all-nerve cluster labelled 'schematic: no Notch', then dissolves so the membrane junction dominates.
scenes.narration: Without Notch, a fly embryo builds too much nervous system and too little skin. How does one cell tell a touching neighbour, “not you”? Its signal never leaves the sending cell.

scenes.tts: Most signals you have met leave the cell that makes them. Notch ligands stay bolted inside the sending cell's membrane. The Notch receptor stays bolted inside the receiving cell right across from it. Because both proteins span their membranes, they usually meet only where two cell surfaces touch.
scenes.caption: Most signals you have met leave the cell that makes them. Notch ligands stay bolted inside the sending cell's membrane. The Notch receptor stays bolted inside the receiving cell right across from it. Because both proteins span their membranes, they usually meet only where two cell surfaces touch.
scenes.visual: In the narrow space between the cells, a warm amber rod labelled 'Ligand' spans the upper membrane, and a cool teal rod labelled 'Notch' spans the lower membrane, with a glowing cyan-teal inner tail extending into the receiving cytosol. Faint drifting dots pass harmlessly by to suggest soluble signals, while the amber ligand and teal Notch glide together until their outer tips latch cleanly.

scenes.tts: Just outside the receiving membrane, Notch folds into a compact lock that hides its cutting spot. Now picture a loose piece of ligand floating freely in solution. It binds Notch with no cell holding on to pull. Will the receptor switch on?
scenes.caption: Just outside the receiving membrane, Notch folds into a compact lock that hides its cutting spot. Now picture a loose piece of ligand floating freely in solution. It binds Notch with no cell holding on to pull. Will the receptor switch on?
scenes.visual: Camera zooms gently onto the lower membrane where bright gold folded modules labelled 'Lock' wrap tightly around the teal Notch stalk just outside the bilayer. The upper cell temporarily recedes; a loose amber ligand fragment drifts in from the left and latches onto the top of teal Notch, bobbing softly with no upward tension. Question card appears at top: 'Loose ligand binds with no pull: does Notch switch on?'
scenes.narration: Just outside the receiving membrane, Notch folds into a compact lock that hides its cutting spot. Now picture a loose piece of ligand floating freely in solution. It binds Notch with no cell holding on to pull. Will the receptor switch on?

scenes.visual: Hold the question card at top for 4.5 seconds while the loose amber fragment bobs gently on teal Notch and the bright gold lock stays closed and gently pulsing. A thin progress bar glides smoothly across the bottom of the question card.

scenes.tts: No. Binding alone leaves the lock shut, so loose ligand generally fails to switch Notch on. In the standard account, the sending cell draws its bound ligand inward by endocytosis. That tug peels the gold lock open.
scenes.caption: No. Binding alone leaves the lock shut, so loose ligand generally fails to switch Notch on. In the standard account, the sending cell draws its bound ligand inward by endocytosis. That tug peels the gold lock open.
scenes.visual: The loose fragment fades and the warm amber sending cell returns above, holding the anchored amber ligand bound to teal Notch. The sending membrane pinches upward into an endocytic pocket, pulling the amber ligand steadily up. Tension lines shimmer along the joined rods; the bright gold lock modules peel outward, revealing a glowing notch mark labelled 'Cut site' just outside the receiving membrane.
scenes.narration: No. Binding alone leaves the lock shut, so loose ligand generally fails to switch Notch on. In the standard account, the sending cell draws its bound ligand inward by endocytosis. That tug peels the gold lock open.

scenes.tts: Mammalian Notch gets one harmless preparation cut while it is made. The two halves stay clasped together. Now the neighbour's pull triggers the active cuts. First, an Adam protease shears the newly exposed site outside the membrane. The outer piece departs upward with the ligand, leaving a short stub.
scenes.caption: Mammalian Notch gets one harmless preparation cut while it is made. The two halves stay clasped together. Now the neighbour's pull triggers the active cuts. First, an ADAM protease shears the newly exposed site outside the membrane. The outer piece departs upward with the ligand, leaving a short stub.
scenes.visual: A brief faint seam mark on the teal outer stalk fades in and out with label 'Prep cut (mammals)' to note the earlier non-signalling cut. Then coral-red shears labelled 'ADAM' glide in from the right and snip the exposed site just outside the membrane. The upper teal outer segment lifts away into the sending cell's pinching vesicle with the amber ligand, leaving only the short transmembrane stub with its cyan-teal inner tail. Empathy fix: Show 'Prep cut: halves stay joined' on the receptor before the active cuts.
scenes.narration: Mammalian Notch gets one harmless preparation cut while it is made. The two halves stay clasped together. Now the neighbour's pull triggers the active cuts. First, an ADAM protease shears the newly exposed site outside the membrane. The outer piece departs upward with the ligand, leaving a short stub.

scenes.tts: Next comes a cut in an unlikely place: inside the oily membrane itself. Gamma secretase accepts a receptor stub only after most of the outer part is trimmed away. Cutting a protein needs water, but the membrane's interior is dry. So presenilin, its cutting subunit, holds its cutting site in a pocket water can reach. It snips the stub, freeing the inner tail.
scenes.caption: Next comes a cut in an unlikely place: inside the oily membrane itself. γ-Secretase accepts a receptor stub only after most of the outer part is trimmed away. Cutting a protein needs water, but the membrane's interior is dry. So presenilin, its cutting subunit, holds its cutting site in a pocket water can reach. It snips the stub, freeing the inner tail.
scenes.visual: A violet ring complex labelled 'γ-Secretase' slides laterally through the receiving membrane to embrace the short teal stub; an inner luminous blue water pocket pulses inside its presenilin core. The stub snaps inside the bilayer. The cyan-teal inner tail, now labelled 'NICD', detaches cleanly from the membrane and begins gliding downward toward the deep indigo nucleus. Empathy fix: Show 'Cut = hydrolysis (needs H2O)' beside the presenilin pocket.
scenes.narration: Next comes a cut in an unlikely place: inside the oily membrane itself. γ-Secretase accepts a receptor stub only after most of the outer part is trimmed away. Cutting a protein needs water, but the membrane's interior is dry. So presenilin, its cutting subunit, holds its cutting site in a pocket water can reach. It snips the stub, freeing the inner tail.

scenes.tts: That freed piece, N I C D, travels directly into the nucleus. In the standard model, C S L sits on target genes with co-repressors holding them off. N I C D binds C S L, displaces co-repressors, and recruits Mastermind. Target genes turn on, and many make repressors that say, not you.
scenes.caption: That freed piece, NICD, travels directly into the nucleus. In the standard model, CSL sits on target genes with co-repressors holding them off. NICD binds CSL, displaces co-repressors, and recruits Mastermind. Target genes turn on, and many make repressors that say, “not you.”
scenes.visual: Follow the glowing cyan-teal NICD continuously down into the deep indigo nucleus, where a slate-grey block labelled 'CSL' sits on a DNA ribbon beside muted grey 'Co-repressors' and a dim gene bar. As NICD docks onto CSL, the grey co-repressors drift away, a bright emerald bar labelled 'Mastermind' snaps into the groove between NICD and CSL, and the gene glows bright emerald, emitting small emerald 'Hes repressors' rising smoothly.
scenes.narration: That freed piece, NICD, travels directly into the nucleus. In the standard model, CSL sits on target genes with co-repressors holding them off. NICD binds CSL, displaces co-repressors, and recruits Mastermind. Target genes turn on, and many make repressors that say, “not you.”

scenes.tts: Here is the rule. A neighbour's pull lets proteases cut one Notch into one nuclear signal. Compare Notch with a kinase cascade. Watch the schematic counters: active kinases multiply the message while the receptor stays intact. Notch has no second messenger and no kinase relay. Each cut receptor is used up once.

scenes.visual: The receiving cell shifts left while a split schematic panel opens smoothly beside it (labelled 'Schematic comparison'). Left side (Notch, teal/cyan): counter ticks '10 pulled -> 10 NICD', intact receptors drop by 10. Right side (Kinase cascade, neutral slate/blue): counter ticks '10 active -> 200 products', intact receptors stay at 10. Both counters animate continuously in sync with the narration.
scenes.narration: Here is the rule. A neighbour's pull lets proteases cut one Notch into one nuclear signal. Compare Notch with a kinase cascade. Watch the schematic counters: active kinases multiply the message while the receptor stays intact. Notch has no second messenger and no kinase relay. Each cut receptor is used up once.

scenes.tts: What the cell buys is a direct, local count of how many receptors a neighbour pulled. The message also stays brief. A nuclear kinase marks the freed tail, ubiquitin tags attach, and the proteasome destroys it. Once pulling stops, no fresh tails arrive, and many direct target genes soon go quiet.

scenes.visual: Zoom back smoothly into the receiving cell's deep indigo nucleus. Bright amber-red tag beads dot the tail of cyan-teal NICD; a barrel-shaped proteasome cartoon draws the tagged NICD in and dissolves it into faint fading specks. Without fresh cyan NICD arriving from the membrane above, the emerald target gene smoothly dims back to quiet slate.
